lines.content: # AB4 - Contact Manager for NUS Students
This keyboard-first contact manager helps NUS students record and retrieve contacts using remembered relationship context. It uses typed commands as its main interaction method and works offline.
- Add contacts with names, contact information, tags, and notes.
- Find contacts using remembered information across names, contact information, tags, and notes.
- Save and restore contact data locally.
See the [User Guide](docs/UserGuide.md) for usage instructions and the [Developer Guide](docs/DeveloperGuide.md) for technical documentation.
This project is based on the AddressBook-Level3 project created by the [SE-EDU initiative](https://se-education.org).

The following provides a quick overview of the main components and their interactions.

**`Main`** (consisting of classes [`Main`](https://github.com/se-edu/addressbook-level3/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/Main.java) and [`MainApp`](https://github.com/se-edu/addressbook-level3/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/MainApp.java)) is in charge of the app launch and shut down.
* At app launch, it initializes the other components in the correct sequence, and connects them up with each other.
* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.
The bulk of the app's work is done by the following four components:
* [**`Model`**](#model-component): Holds the data of the App in memory.
* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.
[**`Commons`**](#common-classes) represents a collection of classes used by multiple other components.
**How the architecture components interact with each other**
The *Sequence Diagram* below shows how the components interact with each other for the scenario where the user issues the command `delete 1`.
Each of the four main components (also shown in the diagram above),
* defines its *API* in an `interface` with the same name as the Component.
* provides its functionality through a concrete `{Component Name}Manager` class that implements the corresponding API interface.

For example, the `Logic` component defines its API in `Logic.java` and implements it in `LogicManager.java`. Other components interact with a component through its interface rather than its concrete class, preventing them from coupling to that component's implementation, as illustrated in the following partial class diagram.
The sections below give more details of each component.
The **API** of this component is specified in [`Ui.java`](https://github.com/se-edu/addressbook-level3/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/Ui.java)

The UI consists of a `MainWindow` and its parts, such as `CommandBox`, `ResultDisplay`, `PersonListPanel`, and `StatusBarFooter`. All of these, including `MainWindow`, inherit from the abstract `UiPart` class, which captures common behavior among classes that represent visible GUI parts.
`CommandBox` uses `CommandHistory` to record non-empty commands submitted during the current application session and
to navigate them with the Up and Down arrow keys. This history belongs to the UI component because it records command
input rather than address-book data; it does not pass through `Logic`, `Model`, or `Storage`.

The `UI` component uses the JavaFX UI framework. The layouts of these UI parts are defined in matching `.fxml` files in `src/main/resources/view`. For example, [`MainWindow.fxml`](https://github.com/se-edu/addressbook-level3/tree/master/src/main/resources/view/MainWindow.fxml) specifies the layout of [`MainWindow`](https://github.com/se-edu/addressbook-level3/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/MainWindow.java).
* executes user commands using the `Logic` component.
* listens for changes to `Model` data so that the UI can be updated with the modified data.
* keeps a reference to the `Logic` component, because the `UI` relies on the `Logic` to execute commands.
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component because it displays `Person` objects from the model.

`MainWindow.refreshActiveSection` updates the active-section label, rebinds `PersonListPanel` to the selected collection's filtered list, and updates the footer's save path after successful commands. Section switching is command-only; the label does not handle clicks.

Here are the other classes in `Logic` (omitted from the class diagram above) that are used for parsing a user command:

* When called upon to parse a user command, the `AddressBookParser` class creates an `XYZCommandParser` (`XYZ` is a placeholder for the specific command name, e.g., `AddCommandParser`). The parser uses the other classes shown above to parse the user command and create an `XYZCommand` object (e.g., `AddCommand`). The `AddressBookParser` returns that object as a `Command` object.

* All `XYZCommandParser` classes, such as `AddCommandParser` and `DeleteCommandParser`, implement the `Parser` interface so they can be treated similarly where appropriate, for example during testing.
* stores independent Contacts and Favourites address books, keyed by `ContactSection`, each with its own `UniquePersonList` of `Person` objects.

* stores the `Person` objects selected by the current filter, such as search results, in a separate _filtered_ list. It exposes this list as an unmodifiable `ObservableList<Person>` that the UI can observe and bind to, so the UI updates when the list changes.
* stores a `UserPrefs` object that represents the user’s preferences (currently, just the GUI settings). This is exposed to the outside as a `ReadOnlyUserPrefs` object.

This section describes some noteworthy details on how certain features are implemented.

`DeleteCommandParser` checks argument count, then delegates ASCII positive-integer validation to `ParserUtil.parsePositiveInteger`. A `BigInteger` retains oversized inputs until empty-list and range validation; conversion to an `int` occurs only after checking the displayed count.

`DeleteCommand` extends `UndoableCommand` and implements `StagedCommand`. Its `prepare` method resolves the displayed index once and returns a `PreparedChange`: a full candidate collection, an operation capturing the selected contact, success feedback, and the save-error message. `LogicManager` saves the candidate before applying that operation. Deletions in Contacts also register an undo snapshot; deletions in Favourites do not. It depends on the staging interface, not a concrete deletion command. A failed save produces no observable live-model changes. Both staging paths require synchronous execution without intervening commands.

The existing duplicate rules remain owned by contact creation. Deletion removes the selected contact object; it does not search by name. Notes are part of that immutable contact, and other contacts retain their own tags and notes.

`CommandBox` clears input only after successful execution and retains it when parsing or execution throws. `PersonListPanel` provides the empty-list placeholder and updates card numbering when cell indices change.

`DeleteUiTest` checks the empty-list label, renumbered cells, and command-input behavior on the JavaFX application thread. Run it with `./gradlew test --tests '*DeleteUiTest'` on a machine with a graphical display. It is skipped on Linux when `DISPLAY` is absent; logic/storage tests remain independent of the display.

The persistent contact-details panel is owned by the view feature and is not yet implemented: `view` currently writes details into the feedback box. Clearing details for the deleted contact, preserving another contact's details, and retaining details on failure remain integration acceptance criteria for that owner. F4 does not add a competing panel.
`ViewCommandParser` requires exactly one argument and parses it as a positive index via `ParserUtil.parseIndex`. Invalid formats surface as `ParseException` with the `view` usage message.

`ViewCommand` does not mutate contacts or trigger a save. It reads `Model#getFilteredPersonList()`, so the index refers to the currently displayed list (including results after `find` or `filter`). An empty displayed list or an out-of-range index raises `CommandException`. On success, it formats the selected contact's fields, tags, and optional note into a `CommandResult` shown in the result box.

`CommandHistory` records every non-empty command submitted from `CommandBox`, including commands that later fail
parsing or execution. Recording occurs before `CommandExecutor.execute` is called. Therefore, a user can recall and
correct an invalid command instead of typing it again. Empty input is ignored and is not added to history.
* a `List<String>` containing the commands available for navigation during the current session;
* a `nextCommandIndex` identifying the current navigation position; and
* a UTF-8 temporary text file containing the same submitted commands, one command per line.
When a command is added, `CommandHistory` first appends it to the temporary file, then adds it to the in-memory list
and moves `nextCommandIndex` to the position immediately after the newest command. This reset ensures that pressing Up
after submitting a new command recalls that new command, even if the user had previously navigated to an older entry.
- When the user presses Up, `getPreviousCommand` moves the index toward the beginning of the list and returns the
- When the user presses Down, `getNextCommand` moves the index toward the end of the list and returns the newer
- `CommandBox` replaces the input text with the returned command and places the caret at the end of that text.
- If the index is already at the oldest or newest available command, the corresponding method returns an empty
`Optional`; the input remains unchanged. Down does not clear the newest command or restore an earlier draft.
The arrow-key event is consumed after history navigation so the `TextField` does not also apply its default key
behavior. Other key events are left untouched.
The default `CommandHistory` constructor creates a new file in the operating system's temporary directory using
`Files.createTempFile`. The file starts empty and is registered for deletion when the JVM exits normally. Every launch
creates a different empty file, so command history is never restored in a later session. It is deliberately separate
from `data/addressbook.json` and the `Storage` component. If appending to the temporary file fails, `CommandBox` logs a
warning and still executes the submitted command; the failed append is not added to the navigable in-memory history.
`CommandHistoryTest` verifies file reset, line-based storage, navigation order and boundaries, and cursor reset
after a new command. `CommandHistoryUiTest` verifies the Up and Down key bindings, caret placement, and retention of a
failed command on the JavaFX application thread. Run them with
`./gradlew test --tests '*CommandHistoryTest' --tests '*CommandHistoryUiTest'`. The UI test is skipped on Linux when
`DISPLAY` is absent; the non-UI history tests remain independent of the display.

`LogicManager` executes commands without the `StagedCommand` capability once against `StagedModel`. The candidate holds both complete collections and uses a snapshot of the visible contacts for indexed operations. It records calls to `addPerson`, `addFavourite`, `setPerson`, `deletePerson`, `setAddressBook`, and view/preference setters. Contact mutations identify the changed section and trigger a save of that collection; unchanged data still saves without adding undo history. View-only commands do not save contact data. A command may change only one collection, enforced by `recordContactChange`, so saving never requires a transaction spanning both files. The current UI runs commands synchronously, so the live model remains unchanged between preparing and committing a command.
After saving, recorded operations are applied to the live model. This preserves incremental list
notifications instead of replacing the whole list for every change. A deletion leaves the live search
predicate active. A rejected command or failed save emits no changes to the live list, preserving UI
selection and the input command. The UI displays success only after `LogicManager.execute` returns.
`JsonAddressBookStorage` serializes UTF-8, pretty-printed JSON to a temporary file in the data directory,
then atomically replaces the destination. It rejects saves if atomic replacement is unavailable and
attempts to clean up temporary files. It never falls back to truncating the original file.

`MainApp` loads both collections independently and always starts on Contacts. A missing Contacts file uses sample contacts; a missing Favourites file uses an empty collection. Loading distinguishes unreadable files, malformed JSON, and invalid contact values. Conversion validates a whole collection before exposing its contacts. A load error starts only the affected collection empty, and `UiManager` reports its section and path after the window opens. If both files fail, both errors are reported. Existing files remain untouched until a command successfully saves a replacement for that collection.
Integration with the other MVP features:
* `JsonAdaptedPerson` saves basic contact fields, tags, and notes. Older files without a note load with
an empty note. Conversion uses the same model validation and duplicate rules as contact commands.
* `view` reads the staged contacts without writing a file. UI updates occur after a successful
`CommandResult`; commands do not directly change UI controls or write storage files.
* `find` and `list` update the view through `Model.updateFilteredPersonList`. Storage always receives
the full address book, never just the displayed results.
* `edit` supports the final `note/` argument with the same parsing and validation as `add`. Other edits
retain the existing note. A failed save leaves the original note and tags untouched.
* Any new Model mutation must also be implemented and recorded by `StagedModel`. Keep `Person` immutable
so copying the collection safely isolates candidate changes. Staging copies both visible membership
and display order, so indexed commands also resolve correctly after `recent`.

`TabCommandParser` accepts exactly `contacts` or `favourites` after trimming surrounding whitespace. `TabCommand` calls `Model.setActiveSection` through staging. This changes the visible collection without marking contact data as changed, so navigation remains available when saving fails. Existing commands keep using the active collection through the `Model` interface. The prepared deletion path also saves the active section's file.

`FavouriteCommandParser` delegates index validation to `ParserUtil.parsePositiveInteger`, retaining a `BigInteger` until the displayed-list range check passes. Missing, extra, or malformed arguments produce the favourite usage message. Execution then validates the active section, empty-list condition, index range, and duplicate identity, in that order.

`FavouriteCommand` selects from the displayed Contacts list and calls `Model.addFavourite`. This appends to Favourites without changing the active section or filter. `StagedModel.getChangedSection()` identifies Favourites as the destination even though Contacts stays active. `LogicManager` saves the full candidate Favourites collection before replaying the append on the live model. Failed saves leave both collections, files, and observable lists unchanged.

Duplicate detection uses `Person.isSamePerson`: matching phone numbers or email addresses. Both files store full contact records, without a favorite flag or cross-file identifier. `Person` is immutable, so sharing its value when copying is safe; later edits replace a record in only one collection. Removing a favorite uses the existing `delete` command while Favourites is active.

The favourites cases in `LogicManagerTest` cover copying a displayed contact, duplicate and selection errors, wrong-section errors, save failure, and context switching with contact commands scoped to the selected collection. `AddressBookParserTest` checks the `favourite` and `tab` command formats. Broader regression testing is deferred to the next milestone. Use the manual scenarios below to verify visible feedback and command-input behavior.

The `undo` command restores Contacts before its most recent successful data-changing command. It keeps at most five full Contacts snapshots for the current application session. Favourites changes do not participate in history, and undo is rejected while Favourites is active. Favourites undo is deferred to the next milestone. Redo and history recovery across restarts are not implemented.

`AddCommand`, `DeleteCommand`, `EditCommand`, and `ClearCommand` extend the abstract `UndoableCommand`. Its `createSnapshot(Model)` helper copies the full pre-command address book, preserving contact order and all fields, including tags and notes. This is a JSON snapshot of model data rather than a diff or a byte-for-byte copy of the existing data file, so it also works before the first data file has been created.

`LogicManager` captures a snapshot only when Contacts is active and the command extends `UndoableCommand`. Both existing execution paths use it: commands executed against `StagedModel`, and commands implementing `StagedCommand` that return a `PreparedChange`. For an undoable Contacts change, `StorageManager.saveUndoableChange(previous, candidate)` delegates to `UndoSnapshotStorage`:
1. Compare the full contact lists. If identical, save the candidate without adding history, then return. This lets `clear` repair an invalid data file when startup has fallen back to an empty model.
1. Save the previous data as a complete JSON backup, then atomically save the candidate as the current data file.
1. Register the backup only after saving succeeds. If history exceeds five entries, remove the oldest entry and attempt to delete its backup.
1. Return to logic, which publishes the prepared changes to the live model.
Changes targeting Favourites, including `FavouriteCommand`, use `Storage.saveFavourites` without recording history.

A rejected command or failed backup/save leaves live contacts and existing history unchanged. Failed commands and unchanged data consume no history slots; view-only commands do not participate in history.

New commands that change Contacts data must extend `UndoableCommand` to participate in undo history. Keep snapshot registration in the shared logic/storage path rather than adding command-specific inverse operations.

The model-level `UndoHistory` interface exposes `readLatestSnapshot()` and `discardLatestSnapshot()` without depending on logic or storage classes. `Storage` extends that interface, and `StorageManager` owns a single `UndoSnapshotStorage` for Contacts. `LogicManager` supplies history to `AddressBookParser`, which passes the narrow interface through `UndoCommandParser` to `UndoCommand`. Parsing does not access history.

1. `prepare(model)` rejects Favourites before accessing Contacts history, then reads the latest snapshot without consuming it. Empty history produces `No changes to undo.`; missing, unreadable, or invalid backup data produces the command's load-error message.
1. The command returns a `PreparedChange` containing the snapshot, success feedback, the undo save-error message, and the operation to apply after saving.
1. The generic staged-command path in `LogicManager` saves the snapshot using `Storage.saveAddressBook`. A failed save leaves the model, filter, current file, and history unchanged.
1. After saving succeeds, the prepared operation replaces the model data, shows all contacts, and consumes the history entry.

`UndoCommand` does not extend `UndoableCommand`, so restoration creates no new history entry. `LogicManager` needs no undo-specific execution branch, and `CommandResult` contains ordinary feedback. Preparation, saving, and application must run synchronously without intervening commands. Callers must use the logic execution path for persistence; directly calling a staged command's `execute` bypasses the save step.

`UndoSnapshotStorage` lazily creates a unique `.addressbook-undo-*` directory beside the address-book file. Its deque stores backup paths, with the latest entry at the end. It removes unused backups after failed saves and attempts cleanup after eviction or consumption. Cleanup errors are logged without reporting an already completed change as a failure.

`MainApp.stop()` calls `Storage.closeUndoHistory()` to clean up Contacts history even if saving preferences fails. Each new session starts with empty history. An abnormal exit can leave backup files on disk; the next session does not recover or reuse them. Persistent history and interrupted-operation recovery are deferred to the next milestone.

Full snapshots avoid command-specific inverse operations and restore contact order and complete records together. The five-entry bound limits active history, but each change serializes the full contact collection. Failed cleanup can leave unreferenced files beyond that bound. Search predicates and GUI preferences are outside snapshots; successful undo deliberately shows all contacts.

The following requirements apply to AB4, the contact manager for NUS students described in the [README](../README.md). They describe the intended product, including requirements that may be implemented after this semester; they are not a statement that the current version satisfies every requirement.

1. **Portability:** AB4 shall run as a standalone desktop application on Windows, macOS, and Linux with only Java `25` installed; compatible JavaFX native libraries shall be bundled. The same release JAR and contact data format shall be usable across these operating systems without changes to application code.

2. **Installation:** After installing the required Java runtime, a user shall be able to launch AB4 from its release JAR without installing a separate database server or application server, or obtaining administrator privileges. The application folder and data location must be writable by the user.

3. **Offline operation:** All contact-management operations shall work without an Internet connection or an online account, including adding, viewing, editing, finding, deleting, saving, and loading contacts and their relationship context.

4. **Capacity:** AB4 shall support at least 1,000 contacts in one address book while meeting the performance requirements below. The evaluation dataset shall include, per contact, a name, phone number, email address, postal address, up to 10 tags of up to 30 characters each, and a note of up to 1,000 characters. These sizes define the evaluation workload, not input validation limits.

5. **Performance:** With the capacity dataset above, at least 95 of 100 consecutive contact-management commands shall display their result within 2 seconds of pressing Enter. Each run shall include adding, listing, viewing, editing, finding, and deleting contacts, with searches covering names, contact information, tags, and notes. Startup shall display the loaded contact list and accept input within 5 seconds. Measure these targets on a computer with at least two CPU cores, 8 GB RAM, and SSD storage, running one AB4 instance with no other resource-intensive applications active.

6. **Keyboard usability:** Typed commands shall be the primary input method, with the GUI providing visual feedback. All contact-management operations shall be completable using the keyboard without mouse interaction. Command results and validation errors shall be visible in the GUI. Invalid input messages shall identify the problem and provide the expected format or permitted values so that users can correct the command.

7. **Learnability:** In a usability evaluation, at least 4 out of 5 NUS students who are comfortable typing commands but have not used AB4 before shall be able to add a contact with relationship context, find that contact, and delete it within 10 minutes in total, using the User Guide without assistance from a facilitator.

8. **Persistence and data integrity:** Following a successful save, all contact fields, tags, and notes shall be preserved across normal shutdown and restart. Rejected commands shall leave contact data unchanged. A failed save or an unreadable or invalid existing data file shall produce a visible error and shall not silently overwrite the last saved data. A save interrupted by an application crash shall leave either the previous complete dataset or the new complete dataset available on disk, rather than a partially written dataset.

9. **Privacy:** AB4 shall store contact data locally and shall not transmit contact details, tags, notes, or entered commands to external services. Diagnostic logs shall not contain these values. Access to local data files is governed by the user's operating-system account and file permissions; this requirement does not imply encryption of the stored data.

10. **Data portability:** Copying a user's saved contact data file to their own computer on another supported operating system running the same AB4 release shall preserve all contact fields, tags, and notes without manual conversion. Contact data shall use a documented, UTF-8 JSON format. If a future release changes that format, it shall document a migration procedure that preserves existing valid data.
11. **Single-user operation:** AB4 shall serve one user, without shared-computer use by different people or routine sharing of data files between users.

12. **Editable storage:** Local JSON data shall remain directly editable in a text editor. Valid edits made while AB4 is closed shall load on restart, including changes to contacts, tags, and notes. The User Guide shall explain the file location, editing procedure, and validation risks, providing at least the editing support described in the [AB3 User Guide](https://se-education.org/addressbook-level3/UserGuide.html#editing-the-data-file). No database management system, including an embedded one, shall store application data.
13. **Distribution:** One JAR, at most 100 MB, shall contain all required dependencies and assets, with no installer or additional software installation beyond Java.

14. **Display compatibility:** The GUI shall avoid resolution-related inconvenience at 1920×1080 or higher with 100% and 125% scaling. All functions shall remain usable at 1280×720 or higher with 150% scaling.
15. **External dependencies:** Third-party dependencies shall be free and permissively licensed; libraries and frameworks shall also be open source.

* **Mainstream OS**: Windows, Linux, Unix, or macOS

* **Address book**: The collection of persons managed by one AB4 instance
* **Person**: A contact record about someone the user wants to remember or contact. In this guide, “person” does not mean the application user
* **Contact information**: Details used to reach a person, such as a phone number, email address, or postal address
* **Relationship context**: Information that helps the user remember how they know a person, such as a shared module, student organisation, project, or event. It can be recorded with tags and notes
* **Tag**: A short label attached to a person to categorise them or record shared context, such as `CS2103T` or `friend`. A person can have more than one tag
* **Note**: Free-text information attached to a person for relationship context that a short tag does not express
* **Group**: A named set of persons, such as a project team or a student-organisation committee. A person can belong to more than one group
* **Availability**: The periods when a person is usually free, stored so the user can coordinate with that person
* **User**: The person operating AB4. The target user is an NUS student who prefers typing commands
* **Index**: The positive integer shown next to a person in the current list. It identifies that person for the current list and is not a permanent identifier
* **MSS**: Main Success Scenario. The steps in a use case in which the actor achieves the intended outcome without taking an extension path

AB4 is a **desktop contact manager for NUS students, optimized for use through a Command Line Interface (CLI)** while retaining the benefits of a Graphical User Interface (GUI). It helps you keep contact details, tags, and notes locally and retrieve contacts by name or tag.

1. Ensure that Java `25` or later is installed on your computer.
**Mac users:** Ensure you have the precise JDK version prescribed [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaInstallationMac.html).
1. Copy the file to the folder you want to use as the _home folder_ for AB4.

1. Open a terminal, `cd` to the folder containing the JAR file, and run `java -jar addressbook.jar`.
A GUI similar to the one below should appear in a few seconds. Note how the app contains some sample data.
1. Type a command in the command box and press Enter to execute it. For example, type **`help`** and press Enter to open the help window.
While typing the command word, you can press **Tab** to autocomplete it. If several commands share the same prefix, press Tab again to cycle through them. Tab does not autocomplete arguments.
Some example commands you can try:
* `list` : Lists all contacts in the active section.
* `recent` : Lists all contacts with the most recently added contact first.
* `add n/John Doe p/98765432 e/johnd@example.com a/John street, block 123, #01-01` : Adds a contact named `John Doe` to the Address Book.
* `delete 3` : Deletes the 3rd contact shown in the current list.
* `favourite 1` : Copies the first displayed contact into Favourites.
* `tab favourites` : Switches to Favourites. Use `tab contacts` to return to Contacts.
* `clear` : Deletes all contacts in the active section.
* `undo` : Restores Contacts before its most recent change in this session.
Press the Up arrow key to fill the command box with an earlier command. Press it repeatedly to move backward through
commands entered during the current launch, and press the Down arrow key to move forward toward newer commands.
Command history is cleared whenever AB4 is launched.
1. Refer to the [Features](#features) section below for details of each command.

* Words in `UPPER_CASE` are the parameters to be supplied by the user.
For example, in `add n/NAME`, replace `NAME` with a value such as `John Doe`.

* Items in square brackets are optional.
For example, `n/NAME [t/TAG]` can be used as `n/John Doe t/friend` or as `n/John Doe`.

* Items followed by `…`​ can appear zero or more times.
For example, `[t/TAG]…​` may be omitted, or written as `t/friend` or `t/friend t/family`.

* Prefixed fields in `add` and `edit` can be in any order, except that `note/NOTE` must be last. For indexed commands such as `edit`, put `INDEX` before the fields.
For example, `add p/91234567 n/John Doe e/john@example.com a/NUS note/Met in class` is valid.

* Extraneous parameters for `help`, `list`, `exit`, and `clear` are ignored.
For example, `help 123` is interpreted as `help`. The `undo` and `recent` commands reject extra parameters.

* Press **Tab** in the command box to autocomplete the command word (the first word only). Matching is case-sensitive. If more than one command matches the typed prefix, Tab cycles through the matches in alphabetical order. After you type a space and start arguments, Tab no longer changes the text.

* If you are using a PDF version of this document, be careful when copying and pasting commands that span multiple lines as space characters surrounding line-breaks may be omitted when copied over to the application.
While the caret is in the command word, press **Tab** to complete it to a known command.
* Matching uses a case-sensitive prefix. For example, `li` + Tab becomes `list`.
* If several commands match, Tab cycles through them. For example, `fi` + Tab cycles between `filter` and `find`.
* Tab does not autocomplete arguments, tags, or prefixes such as `n/` or `t/`.
* Enter still runs whatever text is currently in the command box.
AB4 has two independent collections: **Contacts** and **Favourites**. The application starts on Contacts. The label above the list shows the active section, and the footer shows its data file.
* Switch sections by typing a command; the section label is not a clickable tab.
* `add`, `edit`, `delete`, `clear`, `find`, `filter`, `list`, `recent`, and `view` operate only on the active section. You can also use `add` to create a contact directly in Favourites.
* Switching to a different section shows all contacts there. Returning to a section resets its previous search. Selecting the section that is already active keeps its current search.
* Switching sections does not save or modify contact data. Success shows `Showing Contacts.` or `Showing Favourites.`
* Use the exact lowercase names `contacts` and `favourites`. A missing, unknown, or extra section produces `Invalid command format!` followed by the `tab` usage, without switching sections.
### Marking a contact as a favourite: `favourite`
Copies a contact from Contacts into Favourites, including its phone number, email, address, tags, and note.
* Run this command in Contacts. `INDEX` refers to the currently displayed list, including search results.
* Supply exactly one positive ASCII integer without leading zeros, such as `1` or `12`. Signs, decimals, names, and extra arguments are rejected. Surrounding spaces and tabs are allowed.
* Success appends the copy to Favourites and shows `Added to Favourites: NAME (index INDEX).` Contacts remains selected, its search stays active, and the input clears.
* The copy is independent. Later edits, deletions, and clearing affect only the selected collection. A favourite can remain after its original contact is deleted.
* A contact with the same phone number or email address cannot appear twice in Favourites. Contacts may share the same name. Repeating the command does not update or overwrite the existing favourite.
* To remove a favourite, run `tab favourites` and then `delete INDEX`. You can favourite the original again after removing its copy.
For example, run `tab contacts`, then `find Betsy`, then `favourite 1` to copy the first matching contact. Run `tab favourites` to see the saved copy.
Validation follows the table order. `N` is the number of displayed contacts. Failures retain the entered command and leave both collections unchanged.
| Missing, extra, or malformed index, such as `favourite`, `favourite 1 2`, or `favourite 01` | `Invalid command format!` followed by the `favourite` usage |
| Active section is Favourites | `You are already in Favourites. Switch to Contacts to favourite a contact.` |
| No displayed contacts | `No contacts are displayed. Nothing to favourite.` |
| Index exceeds the displayed count, including an extremely large valid integer | `Contact index out of range. Choose an index from 1 to N.` |
| The phone number or email address already exists in Favourites | `This contact is already in Favourites.` |
| Saving fails | `Could not save changes. No changes were applied. Please try again.` |

A person can have any number of tags, including zero.

The optional `note/` prefix is case-insensitive and must be the final prefix in the command. Notes are trimmed and must contain 1–1000 printable Unicode characters, with no line breaks or control characters.
* `add n/John Doe p/98765432 e/johnd@example.com a/John street, block 123, #01-01`
* `add n/Betsy Crowe t/friend e/betsycrowe@example.com a/Newgate Prison p/1234567 t/criminal`
* `add n/John Doe p/98765432 e/johnd@example.com a/John street note/Known through a dating app`
### Creating and deleting groups, and changing their members: `group`
Create an empty group, then add or remove contacts by their exact names. The contact must already exist in the address book. Group names are case sensitive and must be unique.
Groups and their memberships are saved with the contacts. Deleting a group removes its memberships but keeps the contacts. Deleting a contact also removes it from its groups.
Shows a list of all persons in the active section.
Shows all contacts with the most recently added contact first.
* Addition order is based on the order in which contacts were added. Editing a contact does not make it recent again.
* Deleted contacts are omitted. Commands such as `find`, `list`, and `view` do not change addition order.
* The ordering is preserved after restarting the application.
* If there are no contacts, the command shows `No contacts available.`
* The command does not accept parameters.
Example: After adding `John Doe` and then `Betsy Crowe`, `recent` displays Betsy before John.
Shows the full details of the person at the specified index. The person is not added, edited, or deleted.
* The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed person list. The index **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, …​
* After `find`, the index refers to the filtered list on screen.
* Leading and trailing spaces are ignored, so `view 1` and `view    1` show the same person.

* The result lists name, phone, email, and address. A stored note is included as `Note: NOTE`. A person with no note omits that line. Tags are listed in alphabetical order, separated by commas. A person with no tags shows `Tags: Not specified`.
* The result ends with `Showing details for NAME.`
* `view 1` shows the first person in the displayed list.
* `find Betsy` followed by `view 1` shows the first person in the search results.
| Missing index, extra words, or a value that is not a positive integer, such as `view`, `view 1 John`, `view 0`, or `view Alice` | `Invalid command format!` followed by the `view` usage |
| No contacts are displayed | `No contacts available to view.` |
| Index exceeds the displayed list, including a very large positive integer such as `view 2147483648` | `Invalid index. Please select an index shown in the contact list.` |
Edits an existing person in the active section.
* Edits the person at the specified `INDEX`. The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed person list. The index **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, …​
* At least one of the optional fields must be provided.
* Existing values will be updated to the input values.
* Editing keeps the current `find` or `filter` results. A contact that no longer matches disappears from that list, and the other matches stay. Use `list` to show every contact again.
* When editing tags, all of the person's existing tags are removed; adding tags is not cumulative.
* To remove all of a person's tags, enter `t/` without a tag after it.
* To replace a note, use `note/NOTE` as the final argument, following the same rules as `add`. Omitting it preserves the existing note. For example: `edit 1 note/Discussed frontend implementation`.
* `edit 1 p/91234567 e/johndoe@example.com` Edits the phone number and email address of the 1st person to be `91234567` and `johndoe@example.com` respectively.
* `edit 2 n/Betsy Crower t/` Edits the name of the 2nd person to be `Betsy Crower` and clears all existing tags.
### Locating persons by name, tag, or note: `find`
Finds persons in the active section whose names, tags, or notes contain any of the given keywords.
* The search is case-insensitive; for example, `hans` matches `Hans`.
* Keyword order does not matter; for example, `Hans Bo` matches `Bo Hans`.
* The search considers names, tags, and notes only.
* Only full words match; for example, `Han` does not match `Hans`.
* Persons matching at least one keyword are returned (an `OR` search); for example, `Hans Bo` returns `Hans Gruber` and `Bo Yang`.
* `find John` returns contacts named `john` or `John Doe`, as well as contacts tagged `John`.
Shows persons who have all of the given tags.
* Tag matching is case-insensitive; for example, `t/friends` matches `Friends`.
* Only whole tags match; for example, `t/friend` does not match `friends`.
* If more than one tag is given, a person must have every listed tag.

* While a filter is active, the heading above the contact list shows `Active filter: TAG`. It remains visible after commands such as `view`. `list`, `find`, `recent`, and switching sections remove it.
* A filter that matches nobody shows `No contacts match the specified tag(s).` The contacts remain saved. Use `list` to show them again.
* The index numbers in the result list can be used by commands such as `view`, `edit`, and `delete`.
* Use `list` to show all persons again.
* `filter t/friends t/owesMoney` returns persons who have both tags.

Removes one contact and its contact details, tags, and notes from the active section. A recent deletion from Contacts can be reversed using [undo](#undoing-a-contact-change-undo) while history is available. Favourites deletions cannot be undone yet. Deleting a favourite does not delete its original in Contacts, and deleting an original does not delete its favourite copy.
Angle brackets mark the required index; do not type the brackets.

* The keyword must be lowercase `delete`. Surrounding spaces/tabs and multiple spaces/tabs between the keyword and index are allowed; whitespace inside an index is rejected.

* Success shows `Deleted contact: NAME (index INDEX).`, using the stored name and the index before deletion. Input clears, the current search remains active, and remaining contacts retain their order and are renumbered from 1. Other contacts and their shared tags are preserved.
* Deleting the last displayed contact shows `No contacts to display.` in the list area. Repeating the command uses the updated numbering and may delete a different contact.
* Failures retain the entered command and leave contacts and search results unchanged. A failed save preserves the previous file and live contacts. Successful changes persist after restarting.
Examples: `delete 3` removes the third displayed contact; `find Betsy` followed by `delete 1` removes the first search result.
Validation follows the table order. `N` is the number of displayed contacts; even an extremely large valid integer receives the empty-list or range response.
| More than one argument | `Expected exactly one contact index.` |
| Invalid format, e.g. `0`, `01`, `-1`, `+1`, `abc` | `Invalid contact index. Enter a positive whole number without leading zeros.` |
| No displayed contacts | `No contacts are displayed. Nothing to delete.` |
| Index exceeds displayed count | `Contact index out of range. Choose an index from 1 to N.` |

delete: Deletes the contact identified by the index number used in the displayed contact list.

Clears all entries from the active section. Clearing Contacts leaves Favourites unchanged, and clearing Favourites leaves Contacts unchanged.

Restores Contacts from before its most recent successful `add`, `delete`, `edit`, or `clear` that changed data. Undo is available only in Contacts; use `tab contacts` to switch. Favourites changes, including the `favourite` command, cannot be undone in this milestone and do not consume Contacts history.
* Use lowercase `undo` with no arguments. Surrounding spaces and tabs are accepted.
* Undo restores all Contacts fields, tags, notes, and contact order, then shows all Contacts. Favourites remains unchanged. The previous search filter is not restored.
* Up to five Contacts changes can be undone, most recent first. A sixth Contacts change removes the oldest available undo entry. Switching tabs and changing Favourites do not consume this history.
* Failed commands, identical edits, and clearing an already empty address book do not consume history. Commands such as `find`, `list`, and `view` leave it unchanged.
* Each successful undo consumes one history entry. Undo itself does not create an entry, and there is no redo command.

If a file cannot be loaded, AB4 displays a startup error naming the affected collection and file, and starts that collection empty. The other collection loads independently. No contacts from an invalid file are loaded. The original file remains on disk until a command successfully saves new data to that collection.
